slides.title: One job, many machines
points: Spark splits a dataset too big for one machine into partitions and runs the same steps on each, in parallel.
You write it once; managed platforms such as Databricks, Amazon EMR or Google Dataproc run the cluster for you.

slides.title: Partitions, waves and the shuffle
points: 1 TB in 128 MB partitions is 8,192 tasks; on 200 cores that's about 41 waves of work.
A filter or a map stays on its machine. A groupBy or a join must move rows with the same key together: the shuffle.
The shuffle crosses the network, so filter and aggregate first and shuffle as little as you can.

slides.title: Zaharia's RDD paper
points: Zaharia and colleagues (NSDI 2012) kept data in memory between steps instead of rereading it from disk.
For iterative algorithms and interactive queries, they report it can improve performance by an order of magnitude.

slides.title: Spark's quick start
points: Follow Spark's quick start: count words in a file, then cache it and run the count twice.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

realWorld.name: Zaharia et al., Resilient Distributed Datasets (NSDI 2012)

newQuestions.stem: A nightly Spark job joins 2 TB of click events to a small table of 300 campaigns, and most of its time goes to the shuffle. What should the team try first?
choices: Broadcast the small campaigns table to every machine, so the large side is joined where it already sits
Add more machines and keep the join as it is
Write the events to one big file first
Run the job twice and keep the faster result
why: A broadcast join sends the small table once to each machine, so the 2 TB never moves across the network.
More machines can help, but the same 2 TB still crosses the network in the shuffle.
One file removes the parallelism Spark depends on.
Runs vary a little; the shuffle stays the cost.
